syllabus.clause: enforce in the query engine, not the application: row filters, column masks and dynamic masking (Snowflake masking/row-access policies, Unity Catalog ABAC, BigQuery row-level security and policy tags, Lake Formation, Trino with Ranger/OPA), the impact on pruning and caching, and bypass paths (direct file reads, extracts, unprotected materialized views).

at.step: Reveal: a policy enforced in the engine applies to every query; an application filter only applies to requests that go through that application
Reveal: all 3,000 rows, measured directly -- nothing stops the query yet
Elaborate: a row-security policy is an expression evaluated before the user's own query conditions
Reveal: exactly 1,000 rows, measured directly -- the policy, not the query, decided
Elaborate: the plan itself changes -- EXPLAIN shows no Filter node before the policy, one after it
Reveal: a superuser bypasses the policy entirely, and so does anyone with the file's path

items.item: Trino's OPA integration documents row filtering and column masking as access decisions a policy engine returns, the same decision/enforcement split taught in the previous topic, applied here at the point the engine actually carries the decision out rather than merely deciding it.

at.out: Trino's own OPA-driven row filter and column mask named only as the enforcement-side counterpart to the previous topic's decision-point model; this topic's own measurement runs against PostgreSQL, not Trino

items.item: Unity Catalog's ABAC policies (the previous topic's own subject) are the attribute-based rules that this topic's row filters and column masks actually enforce in the engine; the two topics describe the same governed-tag mechanism from the decision side and the enforcement side respectively.

at.out: Unity Catalog ABAC's own tag-based policy named only as the decision-side counterpart already covered; this topic's own reel teaches enforcement, not the attribute model itself

items.item: Classification and tags (the data-classification topic) supply the object attributes a row filter or column mask condition reads; without a classification pipeline upstream, a row-security policy has nothing but hard-coded literal values to condition on, which does not scale past a handful of rules.

at.out: the classification pipeline's own role as the upstream input named only; this topic's own measurement uses a literal region condition, not a tag-driven one, to isolate the enforcement mechanism

items.item: File encryption (an earlier topic) is the actual defence against the direct-file-read bypass this topic names: an engine policy cannot stop someone with the storage bucket's path from reading the raw Parquet file, but if that file is encrypted and the reader has no key, the bypass gains nothing readable.

at.out: envelope encryption's own role as the defence against the direct-read bypass named only; this topic's own measurement demonstrates the bypass exists (a superuser query, not a raw file read), not the encryption that defends against it

items.item: A materialized view or any derived/exported copy of masked or filtered data carries whatever values were visible to the role that created it; if that role saw unmasked data, the copy permanently holds unmasked data regardless of what policy later changes on the source table.

at.out: the materialized-view and extract bypass paths named explicitly in the syllabus line but not separately measured; this topic's own measurement covers the superuser bypass as the representative case

items.item: PostgreSQL's row-security feature evaluates independent USING (for visibility) and WITH CHECK (for inserts/updates) expressions, and RESTRICTIVE policies additionally AND together with PERMISSIVE ones rather than OR -- a richer policy-combination model than the single allow/deny condition this topic's own single-policy measurement shows.

BigQuery's column-level access control (policy tags, named alongside row-level security in the same syllabus clause) is a separate mechanism from row-level security: a policy tag restricts which columns a principal can select at all, while a row-level access policy restricts which rows come back, and the two compose on the same table.

at.out: BigQuery's policy-tag column mechanism named only as the column-level half of the same named-engines clause; this topic's own measurement demonstrates row-level filtering, not column-level tagging

items.item: Snowflake's masking policies and row access policies are documented as two separate schema-level object types (Dynamic Data Masking for columns, row access policies for rows), not one unified policy object -- a distinction this topic's own PostgreSQL measurement collapses into a single CREATE POLICY mechanism that covers rows only, since column masking in PostgreSQL itself is conventionally done through a view rather than a first-class policy object.

at.out: Snowflake's own two-object model (masking policy vs row access policy) named only; this topic's own measurement runs PostgreSQL's row-security feature, which has no equivalently named column-masking object

items.item: Trino's OPA-driven batch column masking (named in the previous topic's own sources, distinct from single-column masking) lets one policy response mask several columns at once in a single round trip to the policy engine, reducing the per-query overhead of asking about each masked column separately.

at.out: Trino's batch-column-masking optimisation named only; this topic's own measurement concerns a single row policy's plan cost, not a multi-column masking round trip

items.item: A row-security policy's own cost is not fixed: PostgreSQL's planner can still push a leakproof function ahead of the row-security check specifically because it is proven not to leak, so a policy expression's performance depends on whether its own functions qualify for that exception, not just on whether a policy exists at all.

at.out: the leakproof-function exception's own performance implication named only; this topic's own `EXPLAIN` measurement uses a simple equality condition, which is not itself a leakproof-function case
